advanced.scale_10x_100x: At higher call volume, a missing reset would manifest MUCH faster (the counter accumulates across many more calls per unit time), making this bug class more likely to surface in production load testing than in low-volume manual testing.
advanced.production_improvements: Add a metric that tracks consecutiveFailures over time in production, so a reset-logic regression would show up as an unexpectedly early circuit-open event correlated with a period of otherwise-healthy calls.

question: The DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS default value was never actually exercised by any test before a mutation testing pass caught it. How does a default value escape test coverage like that, and how was it finally verified?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh README mein documented `BK4` bug hai: 'every existing test either used a provider that resolved almost immediately (so any timeout value, including 0, would work) or passed an explicit timeoutMs. Closed with a fake-timers test that confirms a call is still pending just under DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS and settles once that deadline passes.'

Yeh gap kyun exist karta tha: `BreachChecker`'s constructor mein `this.timeoutMs = options.timeoutMs ?? DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS;` hai. Zyada tar tests ek fast, fake provider use karte the jo almost instantly resolve ho jaata -- un tests mein `timeoutMs` ki ACTUAL VALUE kabhi matter nahi karti thi, chahe woh `2000` ho ya `0` ho, provider itni jaldi respond kar deta ki timeout kabhi race hi nahi jeet pata. Baaki tests jo timeout behavior test karte the, woh sab explicit `timeoutMs` pass kar rahe the (jaise `timeoutMs: 500`), toh woh bhi `DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS` ki asli value ko kabhi exercise nahi karte the.

Iska matlab: agar koi mutation `DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS` ki value ko `2000` se `0` ya kisi aur number mein badal deta, SAB tests phir bhi pass ho jaate -- yeh ek classic 'untested default' hai.

Fix is tarah hua: `vi.useFakeTimers()` ke saath, ek provider banaya gaya jo KABHI respond nahi karta (AbortSignal ke respect mein reject karta hai), aur `BreachChecker` ko bina koi `timeoutMs` diye banaya gaya (default use karne ke liye). Phir test ne `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS - 100)` kiya aur assert kiya `settled` abhi bhi `false` hai -- yeh prove karta hai ki default 0 ke near kuch nahi hai. Phir 100ms aage advance karke result settle hone ko confirm kiya. Yeh approach EXACTLY default value ko boundary par test karta hai, bina explicitly uski value hardcode kiye test mein (test khud `DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS` constant import karta hai).
why_needed: Default values aur fallback constants bahut aasani se 'untested' reh jaate hain kyunki tests unhe override kar dete hain ya unki exact value irrelevant ban jaati hai fast mocks ki wajah se -- yeh ek systematic blind spot hai jo candidate ko pehchaanna chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek car ka default cruise-control speed setting jo kabhi test hi nahi hoti kyunki har test-drive mein driver manually speed set kar deta hai -- agar koi factory setting galat ho jaaye, koi test isse kabhi nahi pakdega jab tak koi specifically default-untouched scenario test na kare.
how_it_works: Using a never-resolving provider removes the 'fast provider masks the timeout value' problem, and using the DEFAULT constructor path (no explicit timeoutMs) removes the 'explicit override masks the default' problem. Fake timers let the test assert the exact boundary (just under, then just over) without a real wall-clock wait.
in_this_project: `src/breach-checker.ts::DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS` is the constant; `src/breach-checker.ts::BreachChecker`'s constructor does `this.timeoutMs = options.timeoutMs ?? DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS;`. `test/breach-checker.test.ts`'s test `defaults to ${DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS}ms when no timeoutMs is given` is the fix.
advantages: The test imports the constant itself, so it stays correct even if the default value is later changed
A never-responding provider removes any ambiguity about whether the timeout value actually matters
disadvantages: Writing a deliberately-hanging test double takes more setup than a simple mock that resolves immediately
This class of gap is easy to reintroduce for any FUTURE default constant unless the same pattern is applied deliberately
common_mistakes: Testing default behavior with a fast mock that makes the actual default value irrelevant to the test's outcome
Only testing explicit-override paths and assuming the default path is 'obviously fine' because it is a one-line nullish-coalescing expression
Not asserting the boundary from BOTH sides (just under the default, and just at/over it)
follow_up_questions: What other default constants in this codebase (DEFAULT_COMMIT_TIMEOUT_MS, DEFAULT_SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS) have an equivalent boundary test, and which might not?
Why does the test assert settled is false at DEFAULT - 100 instead of just checking the final result?
How would you find every untested default value in a codebase without manually inspecting each one?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Nullish-coalescing defaults (?? DEFAULT_X) keep constructor code terse, but every such default needs its own dedicated boundary test or it silently escapes coverage -- the terseness and the testing burden are directly linked.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS were silently changed to an unreasonably small value (say 1ms) by a careless refactor, every real production breach-check call could start timing out and degrading to null, masking real breach data as 'unknown' without any test failing.
advanced.alternatives: A linter/static-analysis rule that flags every ?? DEFAULT_X pattern and requires a matching boundary test, versus relying purely on mutation testing to catch it after the fact (slower feedback, but no tooling investment).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This specific bug's impact does not scale with traffic volume -- it is a correctness gap, not a throughput one -- but at higher traffic a wrong default timeout would affect a proportionally larger number of breach checks per second, making the blast radius of going undetected larger.
advanced.production_improvements: Add a convention (and ideally a lint rule) that every exported DEFAULT_* timing constant must have a dedicated fake-timers boundary test, following the exact pattern used here for DEFAULT_BREACH_CHECK_TIMEOUT_MS.

question: This project ran line-by-line mutation testing after every stage and found five genuine test gaps across stages 2 and 3 (a double-delete race, a persisted-snapshot bug, a leaked timer, a circuit-breaker reset bug, and an unexercised default timeout). As a debugging/QA methodology, what does mutation testing give you that code-coverage percentages do not, and how would you introduce it into a team's actual workflow?
answer_hinglish:
Code coverage sirf yeh batata hai ki ek line EXECUTE hui ya nahi jab tests chale. Yeh ek necessary lekin bahut weak signal hai -- is project ke paanch real bugs (S16, S22, W3, CB2, BK4) sab ki lines TECHNICALLY covered thi (woh sab normal test runs mein execute ho rahi thi), par koi assertion unki ABSENCE ko kabhi detect nahi kar paati thi. Yeh exactly woh gap hai jo mutation testing specifically target karta hai: ek line ko DELIBERATELY todo (jaise ek condition hata do, ek comparison invert kar do, ek increment hata do), poora test suite chalao, aur dekho koi test fail hota hai ya nahi. Agar koi test fail nahi hota, aapko pata chal jaata hai ki woh line ka BEHAVIOR kisi bhi assertion se guarded nahi hai, chahe line 'covered' hi kyun na ho.

Paanch examples se pattern dikhta hai: S16 (double-delete) -- single-actor tests kabhi multi-actor defensive check exercise nahi karte. S22 (persisted snapshot) -- tests sirf in-memory result check karte the, kabhi store ko inspect nahi karte the. W3 (leaked timer) -- koi test resource-cleanup ko directly assert nahi karta tha. CB2 (breaker reset) -- 'equivalent mutant': single-failure-type sequences reset logic ko kabhi exercise nahi karti. BK4 (default timeout) -- fast mocks aur explicit overrides default value ko kabhi actually matter nahi karne dete the.

Team workflow mein introduce karne ke liye: main yeh suggest karunga ki mutation testing HAR PR par na chalayein (yeh slow hai -- har mutant ke liye poora suite rerun karna padta hai, N mutants x suite time), balki ek periodic (weekly, ya har milestone/stage completion ke baad, jaisa yahan har stage ke baad kiya gaya) scheduled run ki tarah treat karein, specifically security/concurrency-critical files par target karte hue (jaise yahan sirf `manager.ts`, `crypto.ts`, `circuit-breaker.ts` jaise files par, not every file). Survivors ko triage karo: genuine gap ho toh test likho (jaisa 5 cases mein hua), agar truly unreachable/equivalent code ho (jaisa stage 1 ka dead-code guard aur stage 5 ka RV-reorder case) toh usse document karo aur discard karo, invent mat karo ek fake test uske liye.
why_needed: Senior-level QA strategy discussion yeh test karti hai ki candidate coverage metrics ki limitation samajhta hai aur ek practical, cost-aware tarike se mutation testing ko real team workflow mein introduce kar sakta hai, bina 'run it on every commit' jaisa impractical advice de kar.
real_world_analogy: Ek fire drill jahan sab employees 'evacuation route' use kar lete hain (coverage), par koi kabhi actually check nahi karta ki emergency exit door LOCKED hai ya nahi jab tak koi deliberately usse try na kare (mutation) -- door 'covered' tha har drill mein, bas kabhi locked state mein test nahi hua.
how_it_works: A mutation tool applies one small, deliberate change to the source (flip a comparison, remove a line, change a constant), runs the full test suite against that single mutant, restores the file, and repeats for the next mutant. A mutant that no test catches ('survives') identifies a spot where behavior changed but no assertion noticed.
in_this_project: README.md's 'Mutation checks' section documents 128 deliberate breaks across seven stages, with the five genuine survivors (S16, S22, W3, CB2, BK4) each closed with a new test, and two non-bugs (a stage-1 dead-code guard, a stage-5 malformed/unreachable mutant) correctly discarded rather than force-tested.
advantages: Finds test gaps that are provably real -- a surviving mutant is concrete proof some behavior is unguarded, not a guess
Distinguishes genuine gaps (worth a new test) from dead/unreachable code (worth deleting, not testing) via triage, as this project did twice
disadvantages: Expensive: N mutants means N full test-suite runs, which does not scale to running on every commit for a large codebase
Requires human triage of every survivor -- not every survivor is a real bug (two were correctly discarded here)
common_mistakes: Treating 100% code coverage as sufficient evidence of test quality
Running mutation testing on every PR without scoping it, making CI prohibitively slow
Force-fitting a test onto a surviving mutant that is actually unreachable/equivalent code, instead of recognizing and documenting it as such
follow_up_questions: How would you decide which files in a large codebase are worth running mutation testing against?
What is the difference between a genuine survivor and an 'equivalent mutant,' and how do you tell them apart?
How would you integrate mutation testing results into a team's definition of done for a feature stage?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Running mutation testing per-stage (as this project did) rather than per-PR trades immediacy for practicality -- bugs are found at a coarser grain (end of a feature) rather than at commit time, but the cost of running it stays manageable.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without mutation testing, all five real gaps here (S16, S22, W3, CB2, BK4) would have shipped as silently under-tested code -- each is a real production risk (data loss, unreadable vault, memory leak, false circuit trips, wrong timeout behavior) that normal coverage reporting would never have flagged.
advanced.alternatives: Property-based/randomized testing (which this project also uses via test/invariants.test.ts) catches a different class of bug (unexpected sequences of valid operations) than mutation testing (unguarded single-line behaviors) -- the two techniques are complementary, not substitutes for each other.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: As a codebase grows 10x, running mutation testing against the whole thing becomes impractical; the practical approach scales by targeting only security- and concurrency-critical modules (as this project explicitly did, naming specific files) rather than the entire source tree.
advanced.production_improvements: Schedule mutation testing as a milestone-gate (end of each feature/stage) rather than a per-commit CI step, scope it explicitly to critical files, and require every survivor to be triaged into either a new test or a documented, justified discard before the stage is considered done.

question: A support ticket says: 'I shared a password with a teammate, then changed my master password, and now sharing is completely broken for everyone.' Walk through how you would debug this down to its root cause in this codebase, and how the real fix was verified.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exactly woh class of bug hai jo stage 4 mein explicitly identified aur fixed kiya gaya tha, aur PLAN.md/README dono mein documented hai -- ek real gap jo 'had to be fixed', not hypothetical. Debugging approach step by step:

Step 1, reproduce: `getSharingPublicKey` call karo (keypair generate hota hai, private key vault ki apni key se wrapped), phir `changeMasterPassword` call karo, phir ek NAYA share redeem karne ki koshish karo ya recipient side se dekho. Agar bug present hoti, `redeemShare` ke andar `decrypt(session.key, record.wrappedPrivateKey)` fail ho jaata `DECRYPTION_FAILED` ke saath -- kyunki `session.key` ab NEW master password se derived hai, par `wrappedPrivateKey` abhi bhi OLD key se encrypted tha.

Step 2, root cause samajhna: `changeMasterPassword` ka core job hai har entry ko OLD key se decrypt karna aur NEW key se re-encrypt karna. Sharing keypair ka private key bhi EXACTLY same tarah ek secret hai jo vault ki key se wrapped hai -- comment khud code mein hai: 'The sharing keypair's private key is just another secret encrypted under this vault's key -- it must be re-wrapped here too, or it would silently become permanently unreadable after this rotation.' Yeh is project ki documented SH7 mutation hai: 'the private key is never re-wrapped during a rotation'.

Step 3, fix location pinpoint karna: `changeMasterPassword` mein exactly woh line dhoondo jo har entry ko re-encrypt karti hai, aur verify karo ki WRAPPEDPRIVATEKEY ko bhi SAME commit mein, SAME new key se re-wrapped kiya ja raha hai -- `const rewrappedPrivateKey = record.wrappedPrivateKey ? encrypt(newKey, decrypt(oldKey, record.wrappedPrivateKey)) : null;` aur phir commit + in-memory assignment dono mein yeh field pass ho.

Step 4, verify: `test/sharing-integration.test.ts`'s test 'sharing still works after the sender rotates their master password' end-to-end prove karta hai: getSharingPublicKey -> changeMasterPassword -> ek NAYA share abhi bhi successfully create/redeem ho sakta hai, AUR 'the re-wrapped private key (not the old one) is what actually gets persisted' explicitly store ko inspect karta hai, same `lastPersisted` pattern jo S22 bug ke liye use hua tha.
why_needed: Yeh dikhata hai ki jab bhi naya 'secret state' (jaise sharing keypair ka private key) ek existing secret-rotation flow (changeMasterPassword) ke saath add hota hai, uss rotation flow ko EXPLICITLY update karna padta hai har naye secret ke liye -- yahan missing karna sharing ko PERMANENTLY brick kar deta, silently.
real_world_analogy: Ek ghar jiska maalik apna main lock badal leta hai, par bhool jaata hai ki uske paas ek spare key bhi thi jo safe mein rakhi hui thi, encrypted (locked) purane lock se -- naya lock lagne ke baad woh spare key hamesha ke liye useless ho jaati hai, kyunki uska access point hi badal gaya.
how_it_works: changeMasterPassword re-encrypts every secret tied to the old key (entries, AND the sharing private key) into a fresh snapshot keyed by the new key, all inside one atomic commit, before reassigning any in-memory field -- any secret left out of this re-wrap step becomes permanently unreadable the moment the old key is gone.
in_this_project: `src/manager.ts::changeMasterPassword`'s `rewrappedPrivateKey` computation and its inclusion in both the `commit()` call and the post-commit `record.wrappedPrivateKey = rewrappedPrivateKey;` assignment. `test/sharing-integration.test.ts`'s 'sharing still works after the sender rotates their master password' and 'the re-wrapped private key (not the old one) is what actually gets persisted' are the regression tests.
advantages: Sharing survives a master-password rotation transparently -- no manual re-sharing needed by the user
The fix reuses the exact same decrypt-with-old/encrypt-with-new pattern already used for entries, no new logic class introduced
disadvantages: Any FUTURE secret added to a vault (beyond entries and the sharing private key) must remember to follow this same re-wrap discipline, or it will silently brick the same way
There is no automated check that enforces 'every secret field must be re-wrapped in changeMasterPassword' -- it relies on the developer remembering
common_mistakes: Adding a new secret field to a vault record without updating changeMasterPassword's re-wrap logic
Assuming the private key being 'encrypted' is sufficient without checking WHICH key it is encrypted under after a rotation
Testing sharing and password rotation as separate features without a combined integration test covering both together
follow_up_questions: What error would a user actually see if they tried to redeem a share after the sender rotated their password, before this fix existed?
How would you design a safeguard so a future new secret field cannot be forgotten in this re-wrap logic?
Why is this bug specific to the SENDER's rotation and not the RECIPIENT's?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Storing the sharing private key encrypted under the vault's own key (rather than under a separate, independent key) keeps the key-management model uniform with entries, but means every rotation flow must explicitly know about every such secret, creating an easy-to-miss coupling.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without the fix, every vault that generated a sharing keypair and then rotated its master password would have its sharing capability permanently and silently broken -- NO_SHARING_KEY would not even be the error; it would be DECRYPTION_FAILED on redeemShare's attempt to decrypt the now-unreadable wrapped private key, which is a much more confusing symptom to debug from a support ticket alone.
advanced.alternatives: A design that stores a registry of 'all secret fields needing re-wrap' and iterates it generically during rotation (reducing the chance of forgetting one), versus the current explicit, one-off-per-field approach used here, which is simpler to read but more error-prone as more secrets are added.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This bug's severity does not change with scale, but its BLAST RADIUS does -- at 10x/100x more vaults using sharing, a missed re-wrap on a newly added secret field would silently brick sharing for proportionally more users before anyone noticed, since there is no active monitoring for 'can this vault's wrapped secrets still be decrypted.'
advanced.production_improvements: Add a generic internal list of 'secret fields requiring re-wrap on rotation' that changeMasterPassword iterates instead of hardcoding each one, and add a periodic health-check job that attempts to decrypt each vault's wrapped secrets with its current key to catch this class of corruption proactively rather than only when a user hits it.
